# Goal
 
This exercise brings together everything covered so far in *Introduction to C++* and *Classes in C++* (up to, but not including, **Avoiding Resource Leaks**). It introduces **no new material**: every feature you need is in the slides.
 
You will model a tiny, text-only version of a *Xenon*-like shooter: a spaceship that fires shots at enemies, all living inside a `World` that updates them every frame.
 
::: {.callout-note}
This is the seed of your game engine. The abstract `Entity`, the `World` that owns a `std::vector<Entity*>`, and the `update(deltaTime)` loop are exactly the `Actor`, `Level` and `Game` classes of the project — just without graphics yet. In upcoming lectures you will see how to make the ownership safer; for now, managing `new`/`delete` by hand is part of the exercise.
:::
 
## Concepts practised
 
| Concept | Where you use it |
|---|---|
| Separate compilation (`.hpp` / `.cpp`), include guards | Every class |
| Namespaces | Everything lives in `namespace xenon` |
| `struct` vs `class`, encapsulation, `const` member functions | `Vector2D`, all classes |
| Constructors, member initializer lists, uniform initialization `{}` | All classes |
| Operator overloading | `Vector2D` |
| `enum class` + `switch` | `GunType` |
| Exceptions, preconditions, class invariants | `Gun`, `Enemy`, `World` constructors |
| Composition | `SpaceShip` has a `Gun` |
| Abstract classes, pure virtual functions, virtual destructor | `Entity` |
| Derived classes, `override` | `SpaceShip`, `Shot`, `Enemy` |
| `new` / `delete`, destructors, RAII, `nullptr` | `Gun::fire()`, `World` |
| `dynamic_cast` | `World` queries |
| `constexpr` | Simulation constants |
 
# Exercise 1: The `Vector2D` Type
 
Create `Vector2D.hpp` / `Vector2D.cpp` with a simple concrete type used for **both** positions and velocities:
 
```cpp
namespace xenon {
 
struct Vector2D {
    double x{0.0};
    double y{0.0};
};
 
}
```
 
Overload, following the `complex` example from the slides:
 
- `Vector2D& operator+=(Vector2D other)` — as a member
- `Vector2D operator+(Vector2D a, Vector2D b)` — as a non-member, implemented with `+=`
- `Vector2D operator-(Vector2D a, Vector2D b)`
- `Vector2D operator*(Vector2D v, double s)` and `Vector2D operator*(double s, Vector2D v)`
- `bool operator==(Vector2D a, Vector2D b)` and `operator!=`
- `double length(Vector2D v)` — a plain function using `std::sqrt`
 
With these, movement becomes one readable line: `position += velocity * deltaTime;`
 
# Exercise 2: The Entity Hierarchy
 
## `Entity` (abstract base class)
 
Everything that lives in the world is an `Entity`. It holds the data **common to all entities** and declares the interface that each kind of entity must implement.
 
```cpp
// Entity.hpp
#ifndef XENON_ENTITY_HPP
#define XENON_ENTITY_HPP
 
#include "Vector2D.hpp"
 
namespace xenon {
 
class Entity {
public:
    Entity(Vector2D position, Vector2D velocity);
    virtual ~Entity() = default;
 
    virtual void update(double deltaTime) = 0;   // pure virtual
    virtual void print() const = 0;              // pure virtual
 
    Vector2D getPosition() const;
    Vector2D getVelocity() const;
    void setVelocity(Vector2D velocity);
 
    bool isActive() const;
    void deactivate();
 
    void move(double deltaTime);   // position += velocity * deltaTime
 
private:
    Vector2D position;
    Vector2D velocity;
    bool active{true};
};
 
}
 
#endif
```
 
**Questions to answer in a comment at the top of `Entity.hpp`:**
 
1. Why must the destructor be `virtual`?
2. Why can't you write `Entity e{{0, 0}, {0, 0}};`?
3. Which parts of `Entity` are *interface inheritance* and which are *implementation inheritance*?
 
## `Shot`
 
A projectile. Derives from `Entity`.
 
- Constructed with a position, a velocity and a `power` (`double`).
- `update(deltaTime)` simply moves the shot.
- `print()` shows position and power.
- `double getPower() const`.
 
## `Enemy`
 
Derives from `Entity`. Moves from right to left at constant velocity.
 
- Constructed with a position, a velocity and initial `health` (`double`).
- **Precondition:** health must be positive — otherwise throw `std::invalid_argument`.
- `void takeDamage(double amount)` reduces health; when health reaches 0 or less, the enemy deactivates itself.
- `update(deltaTime)` moves the enemy.
- `print()` shows position and health.
 
## `GunType` and `Gun`
 
Define in `Gun.hpp`:
 
```cpp
enum class GunType { light, medium, heavy };
 
double powerOf(GunType type);   // light = 1, medium = 2, heavy = 4 (use a switch)
```
 
`Gun` is a **concrete** class (it is *not* an `Entity`). It manages type, cooldown and ammunition:
 
| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `Gun(GunType type, double cooldown, int maxAmmo)` | Throws `std::invalid_argument` if `cooldown < 0` or `maxAmmo <= 0` |
| `bool canFire() const` | Cooldown has elapsed **and** there is ammunition |
| `void update(double deltaTime)` | Decreases the remaining cooldown (never below 0) |
| `Shot* fire(Vector2D origin)` | Returns a new `Shot` (created with `new`) moving right, with power `powerOf(type)`; returns `nullptr` if it cannot fire |
| `void reload()` | Restores ammunition to the maximum |
| `void upgrade()` | `light → medium → heavy`; `heavy` stays `heavy` |
| `int getAmmo() const`, `GunType getType() const` | Getters |
 
::: {.callout-tip}
`fire()` allocates the shot but does **not** own it: whoever receives the pointer becomes responsible for deleting it (here, the `World`). Returning `nullptr` is how the gun says "no shot this time". This is the same situation as `read_shape()` in the slides.
:::
 
## `SpaceShip`
 
Derives from `Entity`. **Has a** `Gun` (composition — store it by value).
 
- Constructed with a position and a `Gun`.
- `update(deltaTime)` moves the ship **and** updates its gun.
- `Shot* fire()` asks the gun to fire from the ship's current position.
- `void upgradeGun()`, `void reloadGun()`, `const Gun& getGun() const`.
- `print()` shows position, gun type and ammunition.
 
# Exercise 3: The `World`
 
`World` owns every entity and runs the update loop — like `user()` with its `vector<Shape*>` in the slides, but packaged as a class whose destructor does the cleanup (RAII, as in `Vector`).
 
```cpp
class World {
public:
    World(double width, double height);   // throws if width or height <= 0
    ~World();                             // deletes every entity still owned
 
    void add(Entity* entity);             // World takes ownership; ignores nullptr
    void update(double deltaTime);
    void print() const;
 
    int countShots() const;     // uses dynamic_cast
    int countEnemies() const;   // uses dynamic_cast
    SpaceShip* findShip();      // uses dynamic_cast; nullptr if there is none
 
private:
    std::vector<Entity*> entities;   // World owns these
    double width;
    double height;
};
```
 
::: {.callout-warning}
Do **not** copy a `World` (no pass-by-value, no `World w2 = w1;`). With a vector of raw owning pointers, a copy would share the same entities and both destructors would delete them. You will learn how to forbid or fix this in the *Copy and Move* lecture.
:::
 
`World::update(deltaTime)` must, in this order:
 
1. Call `update(deltaTime)` on every entity (through the `Entity` interface — no casts here).
2. Deactivate every entity whose position is outside `[0, width] × [0, height]`.
3. Delete inactive entities and remove them from the vector.
 
Removing elements while iterating needs care. Use this pattern — a range-`for` would break here:
 
```cpp
for (auto it = entities.begin(); it != entities.end(); ) {
    if (!(*it)->isActive()) {
        delete *it;                // free the entity first...
        it = entities.erase(it);   // ...then drop the pointer from the vector
    }
    else {
        ++it;
    }
}
```
 
Thanks to the virtual destructor in `Entity`, `delete *it` destroys the right derived object.
 
# Exercise 4: The Simulation
 
Write `main.cpp`:
 
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include "World.hpp"
#include "SpaceShip.hpp"
#include "Enemy.hpp"
 
int main() {
    using namespace xenon;
 
    constexpr double fps = 60.0;
    constexpr double deltaTime = 1.0 / fps;
    constexpr double simulationTime = 10.0;
 
    try {
        World world{800.0, 600.0};
 
        world.add(new SpaceShip{Vector2D{100.0, 300.0},
                                Gun{GunType::light, 0.5, 20}});
        world.add(new Enemy{Vector2D{790.0, 300.0},
                            Vector2D{-40.0, 0.0}, 5.0});
 
        // ... simulation loop ...
    }
    catch (const std::invalid_argument& e) {
        std::cerr << "Invalid setup: " << e.what() << "\n";
        return 1;
    }
 
    return 0;
}
```
 
The loop must run for 10 simulated seconds at 60 FPS and:
 
- Every frame: get the ship with `world.findShip()`; if it is not `nullptr`, call `fire()` and pass the result to `world.add(...)` (which ignores `nullptr`). Then call `world.update(deltaTime)`.
- Set the ship's velocity to `{0, 30}` for the first 5 seconds and `{0, -30}` after that.
- At t = 4 s, upgrade the gun. At t = 6 s, reload it.
- Spawn a new enemy every 2 seconds at the right edge, at a height of your choice.
- Every second, print the time, `world.countShots()`, `world.countEnemies()` and the ship's state.
 
Finally, **outside** the main `try`, add a second small `try`/`catch` that deliberately constructs an invalid `Gun` (e.g. `maxAmmo = 0`) and shows that the exception is caught.
 
::: {.callout-important}
`findShip()` returns a raw pointer that **observes** the ship; the `World` still **owns** it. Explain in a comment why `main` must never `delete` that pointer, and why it must not keep it across a call that could remove the ship.
:::
 
# Exercise 5: Extensions (Optional)
 
A. **Collisions.** Add `World::handleCollisions()`, called inside `update()` before removing inactive entities. For every pair (`Shot`, `Enemy`) — found with `dynamic_cast` — if `length(shot.pos - enemy.pos) < 10.0`, the enemy takes damage equal to the shot's power and the shot is deactivated. Print a message when an enemy is destroyed.
 
B. **Enemy kinds.** Derive `Loner` from `Enemy`, which also moves vertically in a zig-zag. Only `update()` needs to `override` — and notice that `World` needs no changes at all.
 
C. **Statistics.** Track total shots fired, enemies destroyed and the maximum number of simultaneous shots.
 
# Rules and Deliverables
 
- Files: `Vector2D`, `Entity`, `Shot`, `Enemy`, `Gun`, `SpaceShip`, `World` (each `.hpp` + `.cpp`), plus `main.cpp`.
- Everything inside `namespace xenon`. No `using namespace` in headers.
- **Every `new` has exactly one matching `delete`.** Only `World` deletes entities — in `update()` when they become inactive, and in its destructor for whatever is left.
- All functions that don't modify the object are `const`. Every overriding function is marked `override`.
- Must compile cleanly with **no warnings** and run with **no AddressSanitizer reports** — it detects memory leaks, double deletes and use-after-delete, so it is your check that ownership is right. How to turn both on depends on your IDE:
  - **Visual Studio Community** (our standard IDE for this course), build a **Debug x64** configuration with:
    - Project Properties → C/C++ → General → **Warning Level** set to `/W4`
    - Project Properties → C/C++ → General → **Enable Address Sanitizer** = `Yes` (equivalent to the `/fsanitize=address` compiler switch), available in VS2019 16.9+ and all VS2022 releases
  - **Xcode** (macOS): create a Command Line Tool project (or add your files to one), then:
    - Target → Build Settings → search "Other Warning Flags" → add `-Wall -Wextra`
    - Product menu → **Scheme → Edit Scheme…** → select the **Run** action → **Diagnostics** tab → check **Address Sanitizer** (and, optionally, **Undefined Behavior Sanitizer**)
    - Build and Run (⌘R); ASan reports appear directly in Xcode's console/issue navigator, pointing at the allocation and the bad access
 
  If you build from a terminal instead (WSL, a Makefile, or `g++`/`clang++` directly — this is also the normal path on macOS without Xcode's GUI), the equivalent command is:
 
  ```bash
  g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address -g *.cpp -o xenon
  # or on macOS: clang++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address -g *.cpp -o xenon
  ```
 
  Whichever you use — Visual Studio, Xcode, or the command line — the requirement is the same: zero warnings, zero sanitizer reports.
 
# Tips
 
- **Build incrementally.** Get `Vector2D` working with a tiny test `main` first, then `Entity` + `Shot`, then the rest.
- **Ownership checklist.** For every pointer in your code, ask: *does this own the object (and must eventually `delete` it), or only look at it?* In this exercise, only `World` owns; everyone else just looks.
- **The `World` should never need to know** what kind of entity it is updating. If you find yourself writing `dynamic_cast` inside `World::update()` (outside the optional collisions), the virtual function is in the wrong place.
 
## Common pitfalls
 
::: {.callout-warning}
- Forgetting the `virtual` destructor in `Entity`
- Forgetting `const` on `print()` in a derived class — with `override`, the compiler will catch it
- Erasing from the vector inside a range-`for`
- Not deactivating out-of-bounds entities (the vector grows forever)
- Erasing an inactive entity from the vector without deleting it (leak)
- Deleting an entity twice, or calling `delete` on the pointer returned by `findShip()`
- Forgetting to write `World::~World()`
- Letting the gun's cooldown go negative, or firing with zero ammo
:::
